newsitem.title: UK: Clarke says Britain now stable, successful economy.
newsitem.headline: Clarke says Britain now stable, successful economy.

text.p: Finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Wednesday painted himself as a level-headed manager of Britain's economy after delivering a budget which ignored calls by right-wingers in his Conservative Party for large tax cuts.

After playing what one newspaper described as "the Tories' (Conservatives') last card" ahead of an election less than six months away, Clarke declared: "We are now a stable, successful economy, and this is a sensible, virtuous budget."

The budget, announced to parliament on Tuesday, contained a voter-pleasing one percentage point cut in the standard rate of income tax to 23 percent and modest increases in spending in the key areas of health and education.
But the cuts were almost balanced by higher taxes on petrol and tobacco products and plans to close tax loopholes and end certain allowances.

"Never forget, good economics is good politics," Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke said in his budget speech in an apparent reproof to Conservative legislators who had insisted only huge tax cuts could rescue their party from deep unpopularity.

Opinion polls put the Conservatives some 20 points behind the opposition Labour Party, with an election due by May 22. No party in British polling history has climbed such a huge electoral mountain in so short a time.

But Clarke, in a BBC radio interview, said once electors contemplated the transformation in the British economy since the Conservatives came to power in 1979 they would see powerful reasons for voting again for the ruling party.

"People listening to us...should just look around and see what's happening in Britain and judge by their own perception," he said. Bookmakers Ladbrokes cut their odds on the Conservatives retaining power to 6-4 from 7-4 after the budget.
Clarke said his budget contained "some good news...some bad news" for ordinary people, but on balance cut the tax burden on the average family.

"Last year, the same mixture produced one of the best economic years we have ever had, and so this budget is going to as well," he said. In his budget, he estimated growth this year at 2.5 percent, rising to 3.5 percent next year.

Labour leader Tony Blair, speaking on the same programme, said his party would not vote against the income tax cut, since voters needed some relief from the higher taxes which the Conservatives have introduced since the last election in 1992.
Blair claimed before the budget that the cumulative effect of various tax rises since 1992 amounted to the equivalent of seven percentage points on income tax.

Labour itself has been careful so far to avoid almost all pledges which could give the Conservatives an opportunity to attack Labour as the party of higher taxation, a ploy they used with devastating effect at the 1992 election.
But Blair insisted: "The idea that there is no difference between the two parties is simply not correct."
The verdict of British newspapers on the budget differed largely according to their known political preferences.
The pro-Labour Guardian commented: "Behind the superficial prudence of the budget is a cynical attempt to use the economy to win the election with scant regard for the consequences."
But the more right-leaning Times said: "The chancellor of the exchequer delivered a solid budget speech that had a little something for everyone without taking risks with the economy."
